Your work will define how the world transacts.Speed and craft compoundOur goal is to get faster as Stripe grows. We also revere craftsmanship and obsess over every detail. The tension between those two operating principles – speed and craft – defines how we work.Better defaults existWe don't assume the best way to do something is the way it's always been done. We rethink from first principles how financial services should work, and welcome new ideas from every corner of the company.Built for the bestWe power the world's most ambitious companies because we're obsessed with their success, rigorous about the details, creative in our approach, and always moving with urgency.We're building the economic infrastructure for AIAI is replatforming the global economy. Stripe is building infrastructure to make it possible, including real-time agent micropayments, protocols that let software transact autonomously and fraud prevention for a new generation of threats. These are just some of the challenges you'll be working on.Around 1.7% of global GDP runs on Stripe.Behind every transaction is something someone here built.Solve the problems that matter at scaleStripe is focused on improving the conditions for economic growth and prosperity. We're seeing less growth in the 21st century than we did in the 20th. In rich countries, slower growth corresponds to less innovation and more fractious politics. In poor countries, it means sustained material deprivation. In either case, we need to do better, and we want your help. We're at the centre of this, and we think the best work is still in front of us. hiring_pages.text: OpportunityCompatibilityEmerging talentOpen rolesOpen rolesCompatibilityWorking at Stripe is not for everyoneNot everyone finds success at Stripe. Those who do tend to share a few things in common.The right people don't always think they're rightSuccessful Stripes are rigorous thinkers who appreciate that things worth doing are rarely simple. We want people who are not afraid to be wrong, who can enthusiastically back proposals they initially opposed and who know how to support decisions with numbers and narrative. We operate in situations of substantial uncertainty and cannot afford either timidity or recklessness. The global financial system can seem like a mystifying domain. It isn't. It's made of people and computers, like many other systems you've worked on. Most Stripes don't come from finance, and they've thrived by bringing fresh perspectives. We want generalists who can parachute anywhere into our operations, learn a new field quickly and execute competently beyond their formal remit. We know that we can't be successful without nurturing the careers of both generalists and experts. People who thrive in high-conflict work environments often do not enjoy the experience here. We try to embrace kindness while still encouraging Stripes to take measured risks and act boldly, even in the absence of consensus.Who is Stripe for?Ambitious buildersWe're building solutions without clear precedent, solving problems with far-reaching consequences. The people here find that energising, preferring the joy of discovery to the comfort of certainty.Adaptable problem solversAI is changing how the global economy works, how our customers work and how Stripes work. The people who thrive here adapt quickly and treat obstacles as opportunities.Rigorous thinkersWe argue from first principles, question assumptions, and don't stop at "good enough."The most successful Stripes are the people who have the intellectual horsepower, the curiosity to learn a very complicated business and the humility to get up every day and realise there's a huge amount of things they don't know.Conor McNamaraHead of EMEAWhat all Stripes have in commonWe're dedicated to our work and optimistic about the world. We believe entrepreneurship and free markets do good, and building what supports them matters. If that's you, read on.Motivated by our missionStripe is on a mission to grow the GDP of the internet.Ask yourself:​Do I see free markets and entrepreneurship as powerful forces for advancing progress?​Does enabling entrepreneurship and helping to unlock the internet economy's full potential seem like a compelling use of my time and talents?Embody our operating principles“Users first” is a cornerstone principle. Our users trust us to provide an essential service, and it's a heavy responsibility that we take very seriously.Ask yourself:​Am I motivated to move mountains to protect and support businesses that depend on Stripe?​Am I driven to overcome obstacles and take on big things to drive progress, or do I feel overwhelmed by the sheer scale and breadth of sometimes nebulous opportunities?Energised by changeThe pace of change at Stripe and in the broader economy is accelerating. You'll work outside your domain, take on problems that didn't exist a year ago and be expected to adapt as quickly as the world does.Ask yourself:​Do I see a fast-moving environment as an opportunity rather than an obstacle?​Am I comfortable taking on problems outside my domain or experience?Collaborative, multidisciplinary workBuilding programmable financial infrastructure from first principles is inherently complex. Well-crafted work indicates care for the user, and beautiful work indicates care for the world.Move with urgency and focusWe move with speed on what matters most and take the time to invest in what will make us faster tomorrow. Whereas many companies get slower until they're eventually mired in mediocrity, we aspire to become the world's fastest company.Collaborate egolesslyWe work as one team: no fiefdoms, no hoarding information, no "not my problem." We question assumptions, debate energetically and abandon ideas when better ones emerge. We're generous with credit and stingy with blame. We learn from mistakes together.Stay curiousStripe is an applied exercise in learning about how businesses tick and how the world works. Since the details and possibilities are infinite, we are always seeking to learn. We're energised by the unfamiliar, preferring the joy of discovery to the comfort of certainty.Obsess over talentIt's every Stripe's responsibility to help hire the best and to push for excellence everywhere. Managers must relentlessly uphold our high talent bar, lead their teams with clarity and context, foster development and ultimately support Stripes in accomplishing the best work of their careers.Our cultureLike all great workplaces, Stripe has its own working culture, with norms that can surprise, delight and occasionally perplex.Friday FiresideFriday Fireside is a weekly Stripe-wide forum hosted by Patrick and John. initial_questions.prompt: Describe a backend system you owned end-to-end for at least 2 years. What were the scale characteristics (QPS, data volume), your specific responsibilities, and the hardest production incident you resolved?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: clear ownership over multiple years, concrete scale numbers, on-call/incident ownership, architectural decisions made and their tradeoffs, evidence of sustained impact rather than task execution.

initial_questions.prompt: Walk through a time you had to evolve a monolithic backend into a more distributed architecture. What drove the change, how did you sequence it, and what broke along the way?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: senior-level judgment on when distribution is warranted, strangler-fig or incremental migration strategy, handling of data consistency and failure modes, honest discussion of setbacks and rollback plans.

initial_questions.prompt: In Node.js, explain the event loop phases and how a CPU-bound task in a request handler affects throughput. How would you fix it?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close phases; microtask vs macrotask ordering; blocking the single thread starves I/O; fixes via worker_threads, child processes, offloading to a queue, or breaking work into chunks.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you structure a large TypeScript backend for type safety across service boundaries? Discuss generics, discriminated unions, and runtime validation.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: strict compiler settings, discriminated unions for state/events, generics for reusable contracts, zod/io-ts style runtime validation at boundaries, avoiding `any`, and how types are shared or generated from schemas.

initial_questions.prompt: A query on a large PostgreSQL table is slow. Walk through your diagnosis: what do you inspect, and what fixes do you consider?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), sequential vs index scans, row estimate errors, missing or unused indexes, index-only scans, partial/covering indexes, statistics and ANALYZE, query rewrites, and when partitioning helps.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain PostgreSQL MVCC and how it interacts with transaction isolation levels. How do you handle a hot-row contention problem?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: tuple versions, xmin/xmax, vacuum and bloat, READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE, serialization failures and retries, and mitigations like SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, advisory locks, or queue-style partitioning.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a distributed job scheduler that guarantees at-least-once execution across multiple nodes. How do you prevent duplicate work and handle node failure?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: leader election or lease-based coordination, idempotency keys, visibility timeouts, fencing tokens, heartbeats and failure detection, and discussion of exactly-once being unattainable without idempotent consumers.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you version and evolve a public REST API without breaking existing clients?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: URI vs header versioning, additive-only changes, deprecation policy and sunset headers, contract tests, backward-compatible schema evolution, and monitoring of client usage before removal.

initial_questions.prompt: In an event-driven system, how do you guarantee ordering and handle duplicate or out-of-order events?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: partition keys and per-key ordering, sequence numbers or versions, idempotent consumers, dedup stores, handling late events, and why global ordering is usually avoided.

initial_questions.prompt: You need to deploy a stateless Node.js service on AWS with high availability. Which services do you use and why?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: ECS/EKS or Lambda, ALB, multi-AZ deployment, RDS with replicas, autoscaling policies, secrets management, and observability via CloudWatch; awareness of cost and operational tradeoffs.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you design IAM and network boundaries for a backend service accessing a database and message broker in AWS?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: least-privilege IAM roles, VPC and private subnets, security groups, VPC endpoints, no public database exposure, secrets via Secrets Manager, and separation of duties between services.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you design a payment flow that must not double-charge a customer on retries?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: idempotency keys sent to the payment provider, storing request/response pairs, state machines for payment status, reconciliation jobs, and careful handling of timeouts where the outcome is unknown.

initial_questions.prompt: What does double-entry bookkeeping mean for a financial ledger, and how would you model it in PostgreSQL?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: every transaction has balanced debits and credits, immutable append-only entries, account balances derived or maintained with constraints, auditability, and why you never mutate historical entries.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain Kafka consumer groups, partitions, and offsets. How do you scale consumption without losing ordering guarantees?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: one consumer per partition within a group, rebalancing behavior, offset commit strategies, at-least-once vs at-most-once, and that ordering holds only within a partition so partition key choice matters.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you prevent message loss and duplicate processing in a Kafka-based pipeline?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: acks=all, replication factor, min.insync.replicas, producer idempotence, transactional producers, manual offset commits after processing, idempotent consumers, and dead-letter topics.

initial_questions.prompt: What Kubernetes primitives do you use to run a reliable stateless service, and how do you configure health and scaling?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: Deployments, readiness vs liveness probes, resource requests/limits, HPA, rolling update strategy, PodDisruptionBudgets, and ConfigMaps/Secrets separation.

initial_questions.prompt: A service in Kubernetes is intermittently failing under load. How do you debug it?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: checking pod restarts and OOMKills, resource limits, probe misconfiguration, HPA behavior, node pressure, DNS/service networking, logs and metrics, and distinguishing application from platform causes.

initial_questions.prompt: Stripe processes massive volumes of financial data. Describe your experience with PostgreSQL in a high-throughput environment. How have you optimized database performance, ensured data integrity, and handled schema migrations?

initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe a system with clear separation of concerns, using REST for synchronous operations and events for asynchronous workflows. initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss specific AWS services (e.g., EC2, S3, RDS, Lambda, SQS, SNS) and how they've used them. initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should provide a specific example of mentoring or leading. They should describe their approach to teaching, providing feedback, and fostering collaboration. Look for empathy, patience, and clear communication. Also assess how they handled disagreements or conflicts.

initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss specific payment flows (e.g., authorization, capture, refunds, chargebacks) and how they handled idempotency, reconciliation, and fraud prevention. They should mention compliance standards like PCI DSS and how they ensured data security. If no direct experience, they should relate transferable skills from other domains.

initial_questions.prompt: Stripe uses Kafka for event streaming. Describe your experience with Kafka. How have you used it to build reliable, scalable event-driven systems?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss Kafka concepts like topics, partitions, consumer groups, and offsets. They should explain how they ensured message ordering, exactly-once semantics, and fault tolerance. Also look for experience with Kafka Streams, Connect, or schema registry.

initial_questions.prompt: Stripe deploys on Kubernetes. Describe your experience with Kubernetes. How have you used it to deploy and manage applications?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss Kubernetes objects like deployments, services, ingress, and config maps. They should explain how they handled scaling, rolling updates, and monitoring. Also look for experience with Helm, operators, and troubleshooting.

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 5+ years of backend engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of roles with increasing responsibility, specific projects, and measurable outcomes. Discuss architecture decisions, scaling challenges, and technologies used over time.

flashcards.front: What are key concepts in TypeScript or Node.js that you should know for a backend role?
flashcards.back: For Node.js: event loop, async/await, streams, clustering, error handling. For TypeScript: types, interfaces, generics, decorators, and integrating with frameworks like Express or NestJS.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL queries for performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, proper indexing (B-tree, GIN, etc.), avoid N+1 queries, use connection pooling, partition large tables, and optimize joins and subqueries.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when designing distributed systems?
flashcards.back: CAP theorem, consistency models, partitioning, replication, fault tolerance, idempotency, and handling network partitions. Use patterns like saga, CQRS, and event sourcing.

flashcards.front: How do REST APIs and event-driven systems differ, and when would you use each?
flashcards.back: REST APIs are synchronous request-response, good for CRUD and immediate feedback. Event-driven systems are asynchronous, decoupled, and scalable, good for real-time processing and microservices communication.

flashcards.front: What AWS services have you used for backend development?
flashcards.back: EC2, Lambda, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, ECS/EKS, CloudWatch. Discuss use cases like serverless, storage, messaging, and monitoring.

flashcards.front: How have you mentored engineers in the past?
flashcards.back: Conduct code reviews, pair programming, design docs, knowledge sharing sessions, and setting growth plans. Provide constructive feedback and encourage ownership.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong communication and collaboration in a remote team?
flashcards.back: Use clear written communication, regular stand-ups, documentation, and active listening. Foster psychological safety and cross-functional collaboration.

flashcards.front: What are key challenges in payments or financial systems?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, consistency, audit trails, PCI compliance, fraud detection, and handling monetary values precisely (use decimal types, avoid floating point).

flashcards.front: What is Kafka and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Use cases: real-time data pipelines, event sourcing, log aggregation. Key concepts: topics, partitions, producers, consumers, consumer groups.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is a container orchestration system. Use cases: deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Key concepts: pods, deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets.

questions.answer_outline: Look for: acks=all, replication factor, min.insync.replicas, producer idempotence, transactional producers, manual offset commits after processing, idempotent consumers, and dead-letter topics.

questions.prompt: What Kubernetes primitives do you use to run a reliable stateless service, and how do you configure health and scaling?
questions.answer_outline: Look for: Deployments, readiness vs liveness probes, resource requests/limits, HPA, rolling update strategy, PodDisruptionBudgets, and ConfigMaps/Secrets separation.

questions.prompt: A service in Kubernetes is intermittently failing under load. How do you debug it?
questions.answer_outline: Look for: checking pod restarts and OOMKills, resource limits, probe misconfiguration, HPA behavior, node pressure, DNS/service networking, logs and metrics, and distinguishing application from platform causes.

questions.prompt: Describe a time when you mentored an engineer who was struggling with a technical or professional challenge. What was the situation, what actions did you take, and what was the outcome?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: Identify the engineer and the specific challenge (e.g., struggling with a new technology, code quality, or communication). Task: Explain your responsibility as a mentor and the goals you set. Action: Detail the steps you took (e.g., pair programming, code reviews, regular check-ins, creating a learning plan). Result: Share the outcome (e.g., improved performance, promotion, successful project delivery) and any lessons learned.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you had to mentor multiple engineers with different skill levels and learning styles. How did you tailor your approach to ensure each person's growth?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: Describe the team context and the diverse group of mentees. Task: Explain the need to adapt mentoring strategies. Action: Outline how you assessed individual needs, customized plans, and provided varied support (e.g., one-on-one sessions, group workshops, stretch assignments). Result: Highlight the collective and individual outcomes, such as increased team capability and successful project completions.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a time when you had to collaborate with a cross-functional team (e.g., product, design, QA) to achieve a common goal. What was your role, and how did you ensure effective communication?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: Describe the project and the cross-functional team. Task: Clarify your role and the communication challenges. Action: Explain how you facilitated communication (e.g., regular meetings, clear documentation, active listening, conflict resolution). Result: Share the outcome (e.g., successful launch, improved process) and what you learned about collaboration.

questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had a disagreement with a colleague or stakeholder about a technical decision. How did you handle the conflict while maintaining a strong working relationship?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: Set the context of the disagreement and the parties involved. Task: Explain what was at stake and your goal to resolve it. Action: Detail how you communicated (e.g., listened to their perspective, presented data, sought compromise, escalated if necessary). Result: Describe the resolution and the impact on the relationship and project.

questions.prompt: Stripe's financial infrastructure handles billions of dollars in transactions. Tell us about a time you built a high-scale backend system using TypeScript or Node.js. What specific challenges did you face at scale, and how did you address them?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe a specific project with clear scale metrics (e.g., requests per second, data volume). They should explain architectural decisions, performance optimizations, and how they ensured reliability. Look for depth in Node.js/TypeScript, such as event loop management, async patterns, and memory usage. They should also highlight their role and impact.

questions.prompt: Stripe processes massive volumes of financial data. Describe your experience with PostgreSQL in a high-throughput environment. How have you optimized database performance, ensured data integrity, and handled schema migrations?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss indexing strategies, query optimization, partitioning, replication, and connection pooling. They should mention tools like pg_stat_statements, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and how they've handled migrations with zero downtime. Also look for understanding of ACID, isolation levels, and how they've dealt with concurrency issues.

questions.prompt: Stripe's systems are distributed and event-driven. Can you walk us through a distributed system you designed that used both REST APIs and event-driven patterns? What were the trade-offs, and how did you ensure consistency and reliability?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe a system with clear separation of concerns, using REST for synchronous operations and events for asynchronous workflows. They should discuss trade-offs like latency vs. consistency, and mechanisms like idempotency, retries, dead-letter queues, and exactly-once processing. Look for understanding of CAP theorem and patterns like saga, CQRS, or event sourcing.

questions.prompt: Stripe runs on AWS and similar cloud platforms. Describe your experience with cloud infrastructure. How have you designed for high availability, scalability, and cost efficiency?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss specific AWS services (e.g., EC2, S3, RDS, Lambda, SQS, SNS) and how they've used them. They should cover multi-AZ deployments, auto-scaling, load balancing, and monitoring. Also look for cost optimization strategies and security best practices.

questions.prompt: At Stripe, mentoring and collaboration are key. Tell us about a time you mentored a junior engineer or led a cross-functional project. How did you ensure effective communication and knowledge transfer?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should provide a specific example of mentoring or leading. They should describe their approach to teaching, providing feedback, and fostering collaboration. Look for empathy, patience, and clear communication. Also assess how they handled disagreements or conflicts.

questions.prompt: Stripe is a payments company. Do you have experience with payments or financial systems? If so, describe a challenge you faced and how you ensured correctness and security.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss specific payment flows (e.g., authorization, capture, refunds, chargebacks) and how they handled idempotency, reconciliation, and fraud prevention. They should mention compliance standards like PCI DSS and how they ensured data security. If no direct experience, they should relate transferable skills from other domains.

questions.prompt: Stripe uses Kafka for event streaming. Describe your experience with Kafka. How have you used it to build reliable, scalable event-driven systems?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss Kafka concepts like topics, partitions, consumer groups, and offsets. They should explain how they ensured message ordering, exactly-once semantics, and fault tolerance. Also look for experience with Kafka Streams, Connect, or schema registry.

questions.prompt: Stripe deploys on Kubernetes. Describe your experience with Kubernetes. How have you used it to deploy and manage applications?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss Kubernetes objects like deployments, services, ingress, and config maps. They should explain how they handled scaling, rolling updates, and monitoring. Also look for experience with Helm, operators, and troubleshooting.

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 5+ years of backend engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of roles with increasing responsibility, specific projects, and measurable outcomes. Discuss architecture decisions, scaling challenges, and technologies used over time.

flashcards.front: What are key concepts in TypeScript or Node.js that you should know for a backend role?
flashcards.back: For Node.js: event loop, async/await, streams, clustering, error handling. For TypeScript: types, interfaces, generics, decorators, and integrating with frameworks like Express or NestJS.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL queries for performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, proper indexing (B-tree, GIN, etc.), avoid N+1 queries, use connection pooling, partition large tables, and optimize joins and subqueries.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when designing distributed systems?
flashcards.back: CAP theorem, consistency models, partitioning, replication, fault tolerance, idempotency, and handling network partitions. Use patterns like saga, CQRS, and event sourcing.

flashcards.front: How do REST APIs and event-driven systems differ, and when would you use each?
flashcards.back: REST APIs are synchronous request-response, good for CRUD and immediate feedback. Event-driven systems are asynchronous, decoupled, and scalable, good for real-time processing and microservices communication.

flashcards.front: What AWS services have you used for backend development?
flashcards.back: EC2, Lambda, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, ECS/EKS, CloudWatch. Discuss use cases like serverless, storage, messaging, and monitoring.

flashcards.front: How have you mentored engineers in the past?
flashcards.back: Conduct code reviews, pair programming, design docs, knowledge sharing sessions, and setting growth plans. Provide constructive feedback and encourage ownership.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong communication and collaboration in a remote team?
flashcards.back: Use clear written communication, regular stand-ups, documentation, and active listening. Foster psychological safety and cross-functional collaboration.

flashcards.front: What are key challenges in payments or financial systems?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, consistency, audit trails, PCI compliance, fraud detection, and handling monetary values precisely (use decimal types, avoid floating point).

flashcards.front: What is Kafka and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Use cases: real-time data pipelines, event sourcing, log aggregation. Key concepts: topics, partitions, producers, consumers, consumer groups.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is a container orchestration system. Use cases: deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Key concepts: pods, deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets.

hiring_pages.text: 👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD👀 README.MD# Building differentShopify is where contradictions create magic. We move with startup speed, but we’ve been around for a minute. We're technical to our core and human in our approach. We're deeply serious and seriously playful, because we know that's how the best work gets done.We give a shit and get shit done. We obsess over problems, and build out loud. We build in hard mode. From the founder in the code to the engineers who move like entrepreneurs. Hack it, break it, make it better. It’s about high agency in high ambiguity. Often starting scrappy, but always shipping polished.This environment transforms people. We raise the floor, while we constantly redefine the ceiling. The bar is high and the pace is fast, but nobody climbs alone. That's how we create extraordinary products for our merchants. That’s how we make commerce better for everyone.Ready to join? Let's go. Already built something the world knows? Skip the line.Let's goSkip the lineMakecommercebetterforeveryone.What we doLife-defining work for you—and entrepreneursWe power commerce at every scale. First-time founders at the kitchen table, global brands with stores on every continent, and everyone with a dream in between. We’re the bridge between cutting-edge technology and real merchant success. One platform, built for everyone. Since 2006, we've grown to ~8,000 employees and powered over $1 trillion in sales for millions of merchants in 175 countries. But the real story isn't in the numbers - it's in dreams realized, communities transformed, industries reimagined.How did we get here, you ask? It started with one programmer who couldn't find the right tool to sell snowboards online - so he built it himself How we buildEveryone at Shopify works on product.(Yes, even the finance team.) Product thinking, combined with our reflexive use of AI, is why our people have superpowers. It’s why we build what our merchants need before they know they need it. In a world where AI can make anything, taste and craft become our differentiator.Dive deeper: Read Tobi's AI memo.Where we hireIt's not where you sit, it's where you shipThe way we work is "Digital by Design". We do our daily work wherever we work best, and drop in to one of our Port offices whenever we feel like it. Our Ports are kinda like clubhouses for Shopifolk. Whether it's Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, New York, or Bellevue, drop in whenever you're in town.We also come together when it's obvious we need to connect. That might be big link ups in big numbers like Shopify's annual Summit in Toronto, where thousands of Shopifolk connect with each other, and our mission. It also might be Hack Days at a Port where we prototype, build, and ship fast.Or maybe it's a few days IRL (what we call: Bursts) to solve gnarly problems that can only be tackled in person. Travel happens about 3x a year, starting with Startup Connections (aka in-person onboarding with your new cohort), Shopify Summit, and at least one Burst.Our culture is built on trust, not location. We hire exceptional people wherever they are, then let them cook.Who we hireThe persistently curiousShopify has a unique personality. We hire builders with the same entrepreneurial spirit as the merchants we serve. Master crafters who know what great looks like. People who keep their identities lightweight. Who ship fast, communicate clearly, and leave things better than they found them. If you're energized by new challenges and measure success by growth - not comfort, then read on.Accept our missionCommerce is a powerful expression of free speech. We use it to cast a vote with every product we buy. You need to care deeply about your work towards our mission to make commerce better for everyone not just those you agree with.Thrive on changeWe’re building products for the long-term to make Shopify a forever company, and that requires an unrelenting pace (the week, not the quarter) and an ability to thrive in an unpredictable environment. You need to be resilient to navigate ambiguity.Chase excellenceJoining our team means working with the most driven crafters who pursue mastery. But growth isn’t just an opportunity, it’s an expectation. With resources to help you, you’ll be pushing yourself out of your comfort zone.Find your QuestJob Postings? If we must…We see job postings as problems that need solving, not seats to fill. Shopify is a company of generalists, because the best ideas come from unexpected places, and those are the ideas our merchants need to win. We connect the best people to our most important work. If you’re reading this, you’re probably like me—spending most of your days in your office, in front of a computer.You probably have fifteen tabs open: one for email, one for Slack, one for Google Docs, and on, and on…But have you ever thought about where these “work tools” came from? Or why there are so many of them?To answer these questions, and to explain why we created Notion, we have to travel back in time.As people flooded to factories during the Industrial Revolution, many tools were invented to ease the management overload.Typewriters replaced illegible handwriting. File cabinets stored more information than any clerk could remember (and also won the gold medal at the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair!)Tools like these paved the way for offices as we know them today.Fast forward to the 1950s, when computers came into the workplace.At first, they were lifeless, room-sized monsters that operated on paper and punch cards. They were used solely for number-crunching.Then something magical happened in the 1970s!A generation of pioneers saw the computer as something far beyond a number-crunching machine. They dreamt a future where computers could amplify imagination (Alan Kay), augment intellect (Doug Engelbart), and expand our thoughts far beyond text on paper (Ted Nelson).A tool unlike anything we have seen before.PlayUh-oh! It looks like your ad blocker is preventing the video from playing.Please watch it on YouTubeBut things didn’t turn out that way. As the legend goes, when Steve Jobs “borrowed” the ideas behind personal computing from Xerox PARC, many subtle, but crucial, differences were lost. Hit play and listen to the man himself.And that’s where we are today.Google Docs made typewriters multiplayer. Dropbox brought file cabinets to the cloud. But conceptually, they evolved little beyond their Industrial Revolution ancestors.We duct-tape everything together with emails, copy/paste, and countless open tabs.That’s where Notion comes in. We want to break away from today’s tools—and bring back some of the ideas of those early pioneers.As a first step, we are blending much of your workflow into an all-in-one workspace. Want a task list? A product roadmap? A design repository? They are now all in one place. You can even customize your own workspace from dozens of building blocks.Solve your problems your way, bounded only by your imagination.Hopefully you’ve gotten a good sense of why we started Notion. Challenging the status quo is not an easy task. Check out the product! Write in! We need early adopters like you to start a movement. See you soon!“The best way to predict the future is to invent it.”Alan Kay, computing pioneerJoin usNotion is based in beautiful downtown San Francisco, with offices around the world. initial_questions.prompt: Describe a software project you led end-to-end over at least 6 months. What were the key technical decisions, trade-offs, and outcomes? How did you handle production incidents?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate 3+ years of hands-on engineering: architecture choices, scaling challenges, incident response, and measurable impact. Look for ownership, collaboration, and lessons learned.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain TypeScript's structural type system and how it differs from nominal typing. Provide an example where this leads to unexpected behavior and how you'd mitigate it.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Structural typing compares shapes, not names. Example: two interfaces with same members are interchangeable. Mitigation: branded types, private fields, or explicit type guards. Candidate should discuss trade-offs.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you design a type-safe API client in TypeScript that infers request and response types from a backend schema (e.g., OpenAPI)? Discuss generics, conditional types, and error handling.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Use generics to parameterize endpoints, conditional types to map schema to TS types, and utility types like Pick/Omit. Error handling via discriminated unions for success/failure. Mention code generation or runtime validation (zod).

initial_questions.prompt: You're building an AI-powered feature that summarizes customer support tickets. Outline the architecture, including model selection, prompt design, and how you'd handle failures or hallucinations.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Architecture: API endpoint -> preprocessing -> LLM call (e.g., GPT-4) -> post-processing -> storage. Prompt design: few-shot examples, system instructions. Failures: retries, fallback models, validation of output, human-in-the-loop. Discuss cost/latency trade-offs.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you evaluate and monitor an AI-powered application in production? Discuss metrics, logging, and feedback loops.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Metrics: accuracy, latency, cost per request, user satisfaction. Logging: input/output pairs, model versions, errors. Feedback loops: user ratings, A/B tests, retraining. Mention drift detection and alerting.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a RESTful API for a task management system. Discuss resource naming, HTTP methods, status codes, and versioning.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Resources: /tasks, /users. Methods: GET (list/retrieve), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE. Status codes: 200, 201, 400, 404, 500. Versioning via URL or headers. Mention pagination, filtering, and HATEOAS optionally.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how you would ensure reliability and fault tolerance in a distributed microservices architecture. Discuss patterns like circuit breakers, retries, and idempotency.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures; retries with exponential backoff; idempotency keys for safe retries; timeouts; bulkheads; service discovery; distributed tracing. Candidate should relate to real experience.

initial_questions.prompt: Compare SQL and NoSQL databases. When would you choose one over the other for a given application? Provide examples.
initial_questions.answer_outline: SQL: structured, ACID, relational; NoSQL: flexible schema, horizontal scaling, eventual consistency. Examples: financial transactions -> SQL; real-time analytics -> NoSQL. Discuss trade-offs in consistency, scalability, and query patterns.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you optimize a slow database query in a production system? Walk through your process from identification to resolution.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Identify via slow query logs, EXPLAIN plans. Optimize: indexes, query rewriting, denormalization, caching, partitioning. Consider read replicas, connection pooling. Measure impact and monitor.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a complex bug you debugged. What was the root cause, and how did you systematically identify and fix it?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should outline steps: reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, test, fix, verify. Look for use of tools (debuggers, logs, profilers) and methodical approach. Emphasize learning and prevention.

initial_questions.prompt: You have a production issue where a service intermittently returns 500 errors under high load. How do you debug it?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Check logs, metrics, traces. Look for resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, connections), race conditions, timeouts. Use load testing, profiling. Consider circuit breakers, rate limiting. Fix and add monitoring.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key considerations when integrating an LLM into an existing application? Discuss prompt engineering, token limits, and cost management.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Prompt engineering: clarity, context, examples. Token limits: truncation, summarization, chunking. Cost: model selection, caching, batching. Also latency, rate limits, fallbacks.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain the components of a RAG system. How would you design one for a domain-specific Q&A application?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Components: document ingestion, chunking, embedding, vector store, retrieval, LLM generation. Design: choose embedding model, chunk size, retrieval strategy (e.g., top-k, hybrid search), re-ranking, prompt with context. Evaluate retrieval and generation quality.

initial_questions.prompt: What are agentic systems? Describe how you would build an agent that can perform multi-step tasks using tools.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Agentic systems: LLM-driven loops with planning, tool use, memory. Build: define tools (APIs), prompt for reasoning (ReAct), execute actions, observe results, iterate. Handle errors, limit steps, ensure safety.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you manage state in a large React application? Compare Context, Redux, and React Query.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Context: simple, for low-frequency updates. Redux: predictable, centralized, for complex state. React Query: server state, caching, background updates. Discuss trade-offs and use cases.

Action: explain how you built relationships, aligned priorities, and resolved any conflicts or miscommunications. Result: share the outcome, including how the collaboration benefited the project and what you learned about working across functions.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to influence stakeholders from multiple functions who had conflicting priorities. How did you get them aligned?

Action: detail the steps you took to understand each stakeholder's perspective, communicate trade-offs, and drive consensus. initial_questions.prompt: Give an example of a time you had to explain a complex or technical concept to a non-technical audience. How did you ensure they understood?

initial_questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to deliver difficult or sensitive information in writing (e.g., a project delay, negative feedback, or a policy change). How did you approach it?

questions.prompt: Describe a software project you led end-to-end over at least 6 months. What were the key technical decisions, trade-offs, and outcomes? How did you handle production incidents?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate 3+ years of hands-on engineering: architecture choices, scaling challenges, incident response, and measurable impact. Look for ownership, collaboration, and lessons learned.

questions.prompt: Explain TypeScript's structural type system and how it differs from nominal typing. Provide an example where this leads to unexpected behavior and how you'd mitigate it.
questions.answer_outline: Structural typing compares shapes, not names. Example: two interfaces with same members are interchangeable. Mitigation: branded types, private fields, or explicit type guards. Candidate should discuss trade-offs.

questions.prompt: How would you design a type-safe API client in TypeScript that infers request and response types from a backend schema (e.g., OpenAPI)? Discuss generics, conditional types, and error handling.
questions.answer_outline: Use generics to parameterize endpoints, conditional types to map schema to TS types, and utility types like Pick/Omit. Error handling via discriminated unions for success/failure. Mention code generation or runtime validation (zod).

questions.prompt: You're building an AI-powered feature that summarizes customer support tickets. Outline the architecture, including model selection, prompt design, and how you'd handle failures or hallucinations.
questions.answer_outline: Architecture: API endpoint -> preprocessing -> LLM call (e.g., GPT-4) -> post-processing -> storage. Prompt design: few-shot examples, system instructions. Failures: retries, fallback models, validation of output, human-in-the-loop. Discuss cost/latency trade-offs.

questions.prompt: How would you evaluate and monitor an AI-powered application in production? Discuss metrics, logging, and feedback loops.
questions.answer_outline: Metrics: accuracy, latency, cost per request, user satisfaction. Logging: input/output pairs, model versions, errors. Feedback loops: user ratings, A/B tests, retraining. Mention drift detection and alerting.

questions.prompt: Design a RESTful API for a task management system. Discuss resource naming, HTTP methods, status codes, and versioning.
questions.answer_outline: Resources: /tasks, /users. Methods: GET (list/retrieve), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE. Status codes: 200, 201, 400, 404, 500. Versioning via URL or headers. Mention pagination, filtering, and HATEOAS optionally.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would ensure reliability and fault tolerance in a distributed microservices architecture. Discuss patterns like circuit breakers, retries, and idempotency.
questions.answer_outline: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures; retries with exponential backoff; idempotency keys for safe retries; timeouts; bulkheads; service discovery; distributed tracing. Candidate should relate to real experience.

questions.prompt: Compare SQL and NoSQL databases. When would you choose one over the other for a given application? Provide examples.
questions.answer_outline: SQL: structured, ACID, relational; NoSQL: flexible schema, horizontal scaling, eventual consistency. Examples: financial transactions -> SQL; real-time analytics -> NoSQL. Discuss trade-offs in consistency, scalability, and query patterns.

questions.prompt: How would you optimize a slow database query in a production system? Walk through your process from identification to resolution.
questions.answer_outline: Identify via slow query logs, EXPLAIN plans. Optimize: indexes, query rewriting, denormalization, caching, partitioning. Consider read replicas, connection pooling. Measure impact and monitor.

questions.prompt: Describe a complex bug you debugged. What was the root cause, and how did you systematically identify and fix it?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should outline steps: reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, test, fix, verify. Look for use of tools (debuggers, logs, profilers) and methodical approach. Emphasize learning and prevention.

questions.prompt: You have a production issue where a service intermittently returns 500 errors under high load. How do you debug it?
questions.answer_outline: Check logs, metrics, traces. Look for resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, connections), race conditions, timeouts. Use load testing, profiling. Consider circuit breakers, rate limiting. Fix and add monitoring.

questions.prompt: What are the key considerations when integrating an LLM into an existing application? Discuss prompt engineering, token limits, and cost management.
questions.answer_outline: Prompt engineering: clarity, context, examples. Token limits: truncation, summarization, chunking. Cost: model selection, caching, batching. Also latency, rate limits, fallbacks.

questions.prompt: Explain the components of a RAG system. How would you design one for a domain-specific Q&A application?
questions.answer_outline: Components: document ingestion, chunking, embedding, vector store, retrieval, LLM generation. Design: choose embedding model, chunk size, retrieval strategy (e.g., top-k, hybrid search), re-ranking, prompt with context. Evaluate retrieval and generation quality.

questions.prompt: What are agentic systems? Describe how you would build an agent that can perform multi-step tasks using tools.
questions.answer_outline: Agentic systems: LLM-driven loops with planning, tool use, memory. Build: define tools (APIs), prompt for reasoning (ReAct), execute actions, observe results, iterate. Handle errors, limit steps, ensure safety.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a distributed system you built or significantly contributed to over at least a year. What were the key architectural decisions, and how did you handle failures and scaling as load increased?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate 4+ years of backend experience by detailing a long-term project. Look for: specific components (services, queues, databases), trade-offs made (consistency vs availability, sync vs async), failure handling (retries, circuit breakers, idempotency), and scaling strategies (sharding, partitioning, horizontal scaling). Strong answers show ownership and iterative improvement based on metrics.

initial_questions.prompt: In a language of your choice (Java, Python, Go, or Node.js), how would you design a service that processes a high volume of events asynchronously while maintaining scalability and fault tolerance?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect language-specific idioms: e.g., Java with Spring Boot and Kafka, Python with asyncio and Celery, Go with goroutines and channels, Node.js with event loop and Bull. Should cover: message queue selection, backpressure, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues, monitoring, and horizontal scaling. Depth in concurrency and distributed patterns is key.

initial_questions.prompt: Given a slow-performing SQL query on a large table, walk through your process to diagnose and optimize it. Include specific techniques and tools you would use.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should mention: EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE, indexing strategies (composite, covering), avoiding SELECT *, reducing joins, partitioning, query rewriting, and understanding of database internals (B-tree, isolation levels). Also consider caching, read replicas, and schema design. Strong answers include real examples and metrics.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain the trade-offs between different database transaction isolation levels and how you would choose one for a high-throughput marketplace application.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Should define levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) and anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads). Discuss performance implications and use cases. For marketplace, likely Read Committed with optimistic locking for inventory, or Serializable for critical sections. Mention distributed transactions if relevant.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a RESTful API for a simple marketplace where users can list items and place orders. Focus on resource modeling, versioning, error handling, and pagination.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect: resource-oriented URLs (e.g., /items, /orders), proper HTTP methods and status codes, versioning strategy (URI or header), pagination (cursor or offset), filtering, sorting, and error response format (e.g., RFC 7807). Also consider idempotency for POST, rate limiting, and authentication. Bonus for discussing HATEOAS or GraphQL alternatives.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you design an API that handles asynchronous processing, such as submitting a job and polling for results? Include caching strategies to reduce load.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Should cover: 202 Accepted with Location header, job status endpoint, webhooks or WebSockets for notifications, idempotency keys. Caching: Redis for job status with TTL, cache invalidation on completion, and using CDN for static results. Discuss trade-offs between polling and push, and how to handle failures.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a scenario where you used caching to improve performance. What caching strategy did you choose and why? How did you handle cache invalidation and consistency?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for: cache-aside, write-through, write-behind, or read-through patterns. Justify choice based on read/write ratio, consistency requirements, and latency. Invalidation strategies: TTL, event-based, versioning. Discuss cache stampede, penetration, and hot keys. Mention tools like Redis, Memcached, or in-memory caches.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you approach testing a distributed system? Describe the types of tests you write and tools you use to ensure reliability and catch regressions.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Should cover: unit tests, integration tests, contract tests, end-to-end tests, and chaos engineering. Mention mocking, test containers, and CI/CD integration. For debugging: logging, tracing (e.g., Jaeger), metrics (Prometheus), and distributed tracing. Strong answers include specific examples of bugs found and fixed.

initial_questions.prompt: You notice a production issue where a service intermittently returns errors under load. How do you debug it? Walk through your steps.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe: checking logs and metrics, reproducing in staging, using profiling tools, analyzing thread dumps or heap dumps, and tracing requests. Look for systematic approach: hypothesize, test, isolate. Mention tools like APM, distributed tracing, and load testing. Emphasize root cause analysis and preventive measures.

initial_questions.prompt: Have you worked on a marketplace or two-sided platform? Describe the unique challenges you faced and how you addressed them.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect: matching supply and demand, trust and safety, payments, search and discovery, and handling peak loads. Discuss specific features like listings, orders, reviews, and recommendations. If no direct experience, look for transferable skills from similar domains (e-commerce, social platforms).

initial_questions.prompt: How would you design a recommendation system for a marketplace? Discuss data sources, algorithms, and how you would evaluate and deploy it.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Should cover: collaborative filtering, content-based, hybrid approaches; data pipelines (batch and real-time); feature engineering; offline evaluation (precision, recall, NDCG); online A/B testing; and deployment (model serving, caching). Consider scalability and cold-start problems.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe your experience with high-scale consumer applications. What were the scale metrics (users, requests per second, data volume) and how did you ensure performance and reliability?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for concrete numbers: millions of users, thousands of RPS, terabytes of data. Discuss: horizontal scaling, load balancing, caching, CDNs, database sharding, and auto-scaling. Mention monitoring, alerting, and incident response. Strong answers show understanding of bottlenecks and capacity planning.

initial_questions.prompt: What is your experience with Kubernetes? Describe how you would deploy and manage a microservices application on Kubernetes, including scaling, monitoring, and troubleshooting.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect: deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets, and persistent volumes. Discuss: horizontal pod autoscaling, resource limits, liveness/readiness probes, logging with EFK, monitoring with Prometheus/Grafana, and debugging with kubectl. Mention CI/CD integration and Helm charts.

initial_questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder. How did you ensure they understood, and what was the outcome?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Situation: describe the stakeholder and the complex concept. Task: you needed to communicate it clearly. Action: explain how you tailored the message, used analogies, checked for understanding, and adapted your approach. Result: state the outcome, such as stakeholder buy-in, a decision made, or improved collaboration.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to deliver difficult or unpopular news to your team or a client. How did you communicate it, and what was the result?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Situation: the difficult news and the audience. Task: you needed to communicate it effectively while maintaining trust. Action: explain how you prepared, chose the channel, framed the message, and handled reactions. Result: the outcome, such as team morale, client relationship, or lessons learned.

initial_questions.prompt: Airbnb's backend services handle millions of requests per day across a global infrastructure. Describe a large-scale distributed system you've built or significantly contributed to. What language(s) did you use, and what were the key architectural decisions you made to ensure scalability and reliability?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for 4+ years of backend experience and proficiency in Java, Python, Go, or Node.js. The candidate should describe a system with distributed components, discuss trade-offs (e.g., consistency vs. availability), and highlight scalability techniques like sharding, replication, or load balancing. They should also mention monitoring and failure handling.

initial_questions.prompt: Designing APIs and managing data are critical at Airbnb. Walk me through a time you designed an API and the underlying database schema. How did you ensure the API was intuitive, and what SQL techniques did you use to optimize performance?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect a clear API design (RESTful or GraphQL) with considerations for versioning, pagination, and error handling. For SQL, look for indexing, normalization/denormalization, query optimization, and understanding of transactions. The candidate should connect API design to database performance.

initial_questions.prompt: Caching and asynchronous processing are essential for Airbnb's high-traffic services. Describe a situation where you implemented caching and asynchronous processing to improve performance. How did you test and debug these components to ensure correctness?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for specific caching strategies (e.g., Redis, Memcached) and async processing (e.g., message queues, background jobs). The candidate should discuss testing approaches like unit tests, integration tests, and load testing, as well as debugging tools and techniques for distributed systems.

initial_questions.prompt: At Airbnb, engineers often collaborate with cross-functional teams. Give an example of a time you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder. How did you ensure understanding and alignment?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Assess communication skills: clarity, empathy, and ability to tailor the message. The candidate should describe the context, their approach (e.g., analogies, visual aids), and the outcome. Look for active listening and feedback incorporation.

initial_questions.prompt: Airbnb's marketplace connects hosts and guests, and recommendations are key to personalization. Have you worked on a marketplace or recommendation system? If so, describe your role and the impact of your work. If not, how would you approach building a recommendation feature for a marketplace like Airbnb?
initial_questions.answer_outline: For marketplace experience, look for understanding of two-sided markets, supply/demand dynamics, and trust. For recommendations, expect knowledge of collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, or hybrid approaches, and metrics like CTR or conversion. If no direct experience, assess problem-solving and ability to learn.

initial_questions.prompt: Airbnb operates at massive scale with Kubernetes. Describe your experience with high-scale consumer applications and Kubernetes. How did you ensure your services were resilient and could handle traffic spikes?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for experience with large user bases (millions+), auto-scaling, and container orchestration. The candidate should discuss Kubernetes concepts like pods, deployments, services, and ingress, as well as resilience patterns (circuit breakers, retries, graceful degradation).

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 4+ years of backend engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight specific projects, roles, and durations where you designed, built, and maintained backend services. Emphasize increasing responsibility and impact over time.

flashcards.front: Which programming languages are commonly used for backend engineering, and how would you showcase proficiency in one?
flashcards.back: Java, Python, Go, or Node.js. Showcase proficiency by discussing projects where you used the language to build scalable systems, solve complex problems, and optimize performance.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when building scalable distributed systems?
flashcards.back: Considerations include partitioning, replication, consistency models, fault tolerance, load balancing, and horizontal scaling. Be ready to discuss trade-offs and real-world examples.

flashcards.front: How would you explain strong SQL and database fundamentals?
flashcards.back: Cover normalization, indexing, query optimization, transactions, ACID properties, and experience with relational databases like PostgreSQL or MySQL. Mention NoSQL if relevant.

flashcards.front: What are best practices for designing APIs?
flashcards.back: Best practices include RESTful principles, versioning, clear documentation, proper status codes, authentication/authorization, rate limiting, and designing for idempotency and scalability.

flashcards.front: How do caching and asynchronous processing improve system performance?
flashcards.back: Caching reduces latency and database load by storing frequently accessed data. Asynchronous processing decouples tasks, improves responsiveness, and handles spikes via queues (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka).

flashcards.front: What strategies ensure strong testing and debugging skills?
flashcards.back: Strategies include unit, integration, and end-to-end testing; test-driven development; using debuggers, logging, and monitoring tools; and conducting root cause analysis.

flashcards.front: How can you demonstrate strong communication skills in a technical interview?
flashcards.back: Clearly explain complex technical concepts, actively listen, ask clarifying questions, and structure answers logically. Provide examples of cross-team collaboration and documentation.

flashcards.front: What is marketplace experience, and how would you highlight it?
flashcards.back: Marketplace experience involves building platforms connecting buyers and sellers, handling payments, search, matching, and trust. Highlight projects with two-sided networks, transaction flows, and scalability challenges.

flashcards.front: What are key aspects of recommendation systems?
flashcards.back: Key aspects include collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, matrix factorization, real-time personalization, and evaluation metrics (e.g., precision, recall). Discuss experience with ML pipelines and A/B testing.

flashcards.front: How would you approach high-scale consumer applications?
flashcards.back: Focus on scalability, low latency, high availability, and cost efficiency. Discuss techniques like sharding, caching, CDNs, auto-scaling, and monitoring for millions of users.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes, and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform for deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Experience includes writing manifests, managing clusters, and implementing CI/CD pipelines.

questions.answer_outline: Expect: matching supply and demand, trust and safety, payments, search and discovery, and handling peak loads. Discuss specific features like listings, orders, reviews, and recommendations. If no direct experience, look for transferable skills from similar domains (e-commerce, social platforms).

questions.prompt: How would you design a recommendation system for a marketplace? Discuss data sources, algorithms, and how you would evaluate and deploy it.
questions.answer_outline: Should cover: collaborative filtering, content-based, hybrid approaches; data pipelines (batch and real-time); feature engineering; offline evaluation (precision, recall, NDCG); online A/B testing; and deployment (model serving, caching). Consider scalability and cold-start problems.

questions.prompt: Describe your experience with high-scale consumer applications. What were the scale metrics (users, requests per second, data volume) and how did you ensure performance and reliability?
questions.answer_outline: Look for concrete numbers: millions of users, thousands of RPS, terabytes of data. Discuss: horizontal scaling, load balancing, caching, CDNs, database sharding, and auto-scaling. Mention monitoring, alerting, and incident response. Strong answers show understanding of bottlenecks and capacity planning.

questions.prompt: What is your experience with Kubernetes? Describe how you would deploy and manage a microservices application on Kubernetes, including scaling, monitoring, and troubleshooting.
questions.answer_outline: Expect: deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets, and persistent volumes. Discuss: horizontal pod autoscaling, resource limits, liveness/readiness probes, logging with EFK, monitoring with Prometheus/Grafana, and debugging with kubectl. Mention CI/CD integration and Helm charts.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder. How did you ensure they understood, and what was the outcome?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: describe the stakeholder and the complex concept. Task: you needed to communicate it clearly. Action: explain how you tailored the message, used analogies, checked for understanding, and adapted your approach. Result: state the outcome, such as stakeholder buy-in, a decision made, or improved collaboration.

questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to deliver difficult or unpopular news to your team or a client. How did you communicate it, and what was the result?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: the difficult news and the audience. Task: you needed to communicate it effectively while maintaining trust. Action: explain how you prepared, chose the channel, framed the message, and handled reactions. Result: the outcome, such as team morale, client relationship, or lessons learned.

questions.prompt: Airbnb's backend services handle millions of requests per day across a global infrastructure. Describe a large-scale distributed system you've built or significantly contributed to. What language(s) did you use, and what were the key architectural decisions you made to ensure scalability and reliability?
questions.answer_outline: Look for 4+ years of backend experience and proficiency in Java, Python, Go, or Node.js. The candidate should describe a system with distributed components, discuss trade-offs (e.g., consistency vs. availability), and highlight scalability techniques like sharding, replication, or load balancing. They should also mention monitoring and failure handling.

questions.prompt: Designing APIs and managing data are critical at Airbnb. Walk me through a time you designed an API and the underlying database schema. How did you ensure the API was intuitive, and what SQL techniques did you use to optimize performance?
questions.answer_outline: Expect a clear API design (RESTful or GraphQL) with considerations for versioning, pagination, and error handling. For SQL, look for indexing, normalization/denormalization, query optimization, and understanding of transactions. The candidate should connect API design to database performance.

questions.prompt: Caching and asynchronous processing are essential for Airbnb's high-traffic services. Describe a situation where you implemented caching and asynchronous processing to improve performance. How did you test and debug these components to ensure correctness?
questions.answer_outline: Look for specific caching strategies (e.g., Redis, Memcached) and async processing (e.g., message queues, background jobs). The candidate should discuss testing approaches like unit tests, integration tests, and load testing, as well as debugging tools and techniques for distributed systems.

questions.prompt: At Airbnb, engineers often collaborate with cross-functional teams. Give an example of a time you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder. How did you ensure understanding and alignment?
questions.answer_outline: Assess communication skills: clarity, empathy, and ability to tailor the message. The candidate should describe the context, their approach (e.g., analogies, visual aids), and the outcome. Look for active listening and feedback incorporation.

questions.prompt: Airbnb's marketplace connects hosts and guests, and recommendations are key to personalization. Have you worked on a marketplace or recommendation system? If so, describe your role and the impact of your work. If not, how would you approach building a recommendation feature for a marketplace like Airbnb?
questions.answer_outline: For marketplace experience, look for understanding of two-sided markets, supply/demand dynamics, and trust. For recommendations, expect knowledge of collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, or hybrid approaches, and metrics like CTR or conversion. If no direct experience, assess problem-solving and ability to learn.

questions.prompt: Airbnb operates at massive scale with Kubernetes. Describe your experience with high-scale consumer applications and Kubernetes. How did you ensure your services were resilient and could handle traffic spikes?
questions.answer_outline: Look for experience with large user bases (millions+), auto-scaling, and container orchestration. The candidate should discuss Kubernetes concepts like pods, deployments, services, and ingress, as well as resilience patterns (circuit breakers, retries, graceful degradation).

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 4+ years of backend engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight specific projects, roles, and durations where you designed, built, and maintained backend services. Emphasize increasing responsibility and impact over time.

flashcards.front: Which programming languages are commonly used for backend engineering, and how would you showcase proficiency in one?
flashcards.back: Java, Python, Go, or Node.js. Showcase proficiency by discussing projects where you used the language to build scalable systems, solve complex problems, and optimize performance.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when building scalable distributed systems?
flashcards.back: Considerations include partitioning, replication, consistency models, fault tolerance, load balancing, and horizontal scaling. Be ready to discuss trade-offs and real-world examples.

flashcards.front: How would you explain strong SQL and database fundamentals?
flashcards.back: Cover normalization, indexing, query optimization, transactions, ACID properties, and experience with relational databases like PostgreSQL or MySQL. Mention NoSQL if relevant.

flashcards.front: What are best practices for designing APIs?
flashcards.back: Best practices include RESTful principles, versioning, clear documentation, proper status codes, authentication/authorization, rate limiting, and designing for idempotency and scalability.

flashcards.front: How do caching and asynchronous processing improve system performance?
flashcards.back: Caching reduces latency and database load by storing frequently accessed data. Asynchronous processing decouples tasks, improves responsiveness, and handles spikes via queues (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka).

flashcards.front: What strategies ensure strong testing and debugging skills?
flashcards.back: Strategies include unit, integration, and end-to-end testing; test-driven development; using debuggers, logging, and monitoring tools; and conducting root cause analysis.

flashcards.front: How can you demonstrate strong communication skills in a technical interview?
flashcards.back: Clearly explain complex technical concepts, actively listen, ask clarifying questions, and structure answers logically. Provide examples of cross-team collaboration and documentation.

flashcards.front: What is marketplace experience, and how would you highlight it?
flashcards.back: Marketplace experience involves building platforms connecting buyers and sellers, handling payments, search, matching, and trust. Highlight projects with two-sided networks, transaction flows, and scalability challenges.

flashcards.front: What are key aspects of recommendation systems?
flashcards.back: Key aspects include collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, matrix factorization, real-time personalization, and evaluation metrics (e.g., precision, recall). Discuss experience with ML pipelines and A/B testing.

flashcards.front: How would you approach high-scale consumer applications?
flashcards.back: Focus on scalability, low latency, high availability, and cost efficiency. Discuss techniques like sharding, caching, CDNs, auto-scaling, and monitoring for millions of users.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes, and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform for deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Experience includes writing manifests, managing clusters, and implementing CI/CD pipelines.
